description: Search and analyze email in Outlook OST/PST files directly on disk (pure Python [MS-PST] reader with a full-text sidecar index; no Outlook, no native dependencies; bounded memory, 10 GB+ stores are fine).
instructions: Read, search and analyze email inside Outlook OST/PST data files directly (no Outlook needed; any OS; the file is never modified). The model invokes it with {"action":"ostparse","command":"SUBCOMMAND [args]"}; the operator types /ostparse SUBCOMMAND [args]. Workflow: first 'open /absolute/path/mailbox.ost' selects the store for this session (no password is needed or accepted — ostparse reads OST/PST content directly; do not warn the user about passwords); then 'search QUERY' answers in milliseconds from a sidecar full-text index (FILE.ostidx) that is built automatically on first search and updated incrementally when the file changes — on a multi-GB store run 'index' once first, it is the only slow step. Subcommands: open FILE (reads any OST/PST directly) | close | info (header/format JSON) | tree (folder hierarchy with message counts and nids) | index [rebuild] | search QUERY [--limit N --offset N --sort date|oldest|size|relevance|subject|from --facet folder|from|domain|year|month|ext|class|size --exact --json --no-snippets] | count QUERY (exact match count) | show NID [--full] [--headers] (one message: addresses, attachments, and the readable text body — plain text, else RTF, else the HTML body stripped to text, so HTML-only mail still shows its content; NID is the nid=0x... token printed by search/tree) | export DIR QUERY [--limit N] (write matching messages as RFC 5322 .eml files) | stats (walk the whole store: folder/message/attachment totals; slow on huge files) | help query (full query syntax). QUERY uses Outlook Instant Search (AQS) syntax plus regex: words are ANDed; "quoted phrase"; OR, NOT, -term, (grouping); fields from: to: cc: bcc: participants: subject: body: attachment:report.pdf ext:pdf in:inbox folder:"sent items"; from:(alice OR bob); wildcards budg* b?dget; /regex/ with flags i c s m x; dates received:/sent:/date: (received:last week, sent:2024-03-15, date:2024-01-01..2024-03-31, received:march 2024, date:>=2026); sizes messagesize:>5MB size:tiny..enormous; flags hasattachment:yes is:unread is:flagged read:no importance:high; kind:email|meetings|contacts; messageclass:ipm.note; nid:0x200024 for one message. Typical investigation: open the file, 'search from:alice hasattachment:yes received:last month \"budget review\"', then 'show 0x200024 --full' to read a hit, 'count QUERY' / '--facet folder' to profile, and 'export ./out QUERY' to hand .eml files to other tools. Results are plain text, one numbered line per hit ending in nid=0x...; page with --offset. Example action: {"action":"ostparse","command":"search in:inbox from:david /inv-\\d{4}/ --limit 10"}. When the user wants to understand, summarize, triage or get a handle on a whole mailbox rather than locate one message, profile it instead of listing messages: use --facet (from, domain, month, folder) with counts to separate real correspondence from bulk newsletters and automated notices, identify the dominant senders and the busiest periods. Then you MUST read several representative message bodies with show before describing what any mail is about: counts and subjects reveal structure, but search lines and snippets are previews, not the body, so never state what a thread, sender or message concerns, or judge its importance, from a subject or snippet alone — open it with show and base the claim on the body you read, citing that nid. Answer with a short narrative of what is going on in this mailbox — the main threads, who matters, what plausibly needs action, and what is just noise — grounded in bodies you actually read and citing specific senders, dates and nids as evidence, not a numbered list or generic buckets. Command output is never clipped. Search --json returns a complete JSON document for the requested page; use --limit and --offset to retrieve additional pages. Search snippets are previews, not complete message bodies. Show returns the full available text body (plain text, RTF, or HTML stripped to text); --full remains accepted for compatibility. Attachments: 'show' and 'export' list each attachment's filename, size and type, and 'export' writes the whole message (attachments included) as a .eml file; this plugin does not read the contents inside an attachment (it will not extract text from a PDF, image or Office file). To act on an attachment, export the message and open the saved file with a tool meant for that type — do not try to parse attachment bytes yourself.
